title: The Ordinary Aftermath
premise: After her mother's funeral, Elodie Winterbourne inventories the silences left behind in the family's coastal house, cataloging what was never said. When a radio plays a song her mother wrote and never recorded, Elodie traces it to Marrow Bay, where a decades-old betrayal — a stolen song, a drowned friend, a town that chose loyalty over truth — still holds everyone in its grip. As she gathers testimony from the living, she must decide whether exposing the truth will honor her mother or destroy the people who protected her. In the end, Elodie chooses justice outside the law: she records the song herself, credits its true author publicly, and lets the town reckon with what it buried.
about_author: Astrid Okonkwo is a former archivist who spent years cataloging unclaimed letters in municipal storage, an experience that shaped her fascination with inherited silence. She writes literary fiction about families, memory, and the small acts of repair that outlast institutions.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Elodie, grieving and precise, catalogs her mother Vivian's silence room by room after the funeral: unopened letters, a locked drawer, a guitar case never opened in thirty years. Her POV establishes her need for order as armor against grief. The emotional beat is controlled sorrow cracking at the edges when she finds a lyric sheet with someone else's name crossed out.

chapters.title: A Song on the Radio
chapters.summary: Driving home, Elodie hears a local station play 'The Ordinary Aftermath' — word for word the lyric sheet she found. The DJ mentions it was written by a woman who died young in Marrow Bay. Elodie's POV; the beat is vertigo, the sense that her careful inventory has just been overturned by something alive.

chapters.title: Marrow Bay
chapters.summary: Elodie arrives in the fading fishing town where her mother grew up, checking into a boarding house run by Ruth Calloway, who recognizes the Winterbourne name and goes quiet. Through Elodie's eyes the town feels rehearsed, everyone performing normalcy. The beat is unease: welcome with a locked door behind it.

chapters.title: The Drowned Girl
chapters.summary: Ruth's brother Amos, drunk and guilt-ridden, tells Elodie about Lena Okafor, Vivian's best friend, who wrote songs and drowned in 1989 — ruled an accident. He hints Vivian knew more than she ever said. His POV chapter; the beat is confession as relief that curdles into fear of who might be listening.

chapters.title: What the Choir Knew
chapters.summary: Elodie interviews the aging church choir, discovering Lena's songs were performed under Pastor Deane's name after her death. The choir members defend the arrangement as mercy for a broken town. Elodie's POV; the beat is her first real anger — theft dressed up as kindness.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed
chapters.summary: Pastor Deane, dying and lucid, admits he registered Lena's songs legally and paid the town's silence with royalties funneled through the church. He claims Vivian begged him to. His POV; the beat is a man mistaking stewardship for ownership, offering Elodie his version of protection.

chapters.title: The Night of the Storm
chapters.summary: Ruth finally breaks: she saw Lena and Vivian argue on the seawall the night Lena died, and saw Deane watching. She has kept it secret forty years to protect her brother Amos, whose car was near the water. Ruth's POV; the beat is loyalty revealed as a cage she built around herself.

chapters.title: Running Out of Tide
chapters.summary: Deane's family, learning of his confessions, moves to have him declared incompetent and the church records sealed; Amos disappears, feared suicidal. Elodie realizes testimony is evaporating faster than she can gather it. Her POV; the beat is desperation sharpened into resolve — truth needs a body, not just witnesses.

chapters.title: The Seawall
chapters.summary: Climax: Elodie finds Amos at the seawall intending to confess and drown himself; she talks him back by promising the truth won't be a courtroom's but the town's own. Confronting Deane's son and the choir together, she plays Lena's demo tape, recovered from the locked drawer, before the whole congregation. The beat is rupture — the town forced to hear what it sang along to.

chapters.title: Everything Said at Last
chapters.summary: Resolution: months later, the songs are re-registered to Lena Okafor's estate; a plaque replaces the sealed record, and Amos, alive, tends Lena's grave. Elodie records 'The Ordinary Aftermath' in her mother's house, crediting both women, and adds a final page to her inventory: everything now said. The beat is quiet, earned peace.
